CLAUDE.md

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

Shared conventions

The portfolio’s shared rules are synced into .claude/shared/ from pedrobtz/packages:claude/shared/. Never edit them here. Where this file and a shared file disagree, this file wins for zucrypt.

@.claude/shared/workflow.md @.claude/shared/r-package.md @.claude/shared/ci.md @.claude/shared/native-code.md @.claude/shared/correctness.md @.claude/shared/assurance.md

What this is

zucrypt is cryptography over raw vectors with no system library: a vendored, pinned TF-PSA-Crypto subset (the Mbed TLS project’s cryptography library) built from source, exposed to R as crypt_* functions and to other packages as a static archive and a registered C table. It is one package in the zu* family (siblings are checked out alongside it: zuxlsx, zuxml, zukomp, zuhttp, zujwt, …). Design revision 4 widened it from zuxlsx’s archive provider into an alternative to the openssl package, through an openssl-shaped layer (design §7.1) added in tranches after v0.1.0. A primitive enters on the admission rule of design §6 (a numbered standard, published vectors, an outside oracle, a composition contract, a demonstrated workflow benefit), not on a named consumer.

The boundary is strict and is the main thing to preserve:

  • zucrypt owns cryptography: hashes, HMAC, AES, randomness, AEAD, KDFs, keys, signatures and, from Stage 17, certificate data; and, if Stage 18 is taken, a TLS client engine for zuhttp (design §10). It never acquires XML, ZIP, Office, socket, name-resolution, proxy or trust-store dependencies, and never reaches the user’s environment (no key files, passphrase prompts or certificate downloads: design §5).
  • Office/Excel decryption orchestration lives in zuxlsx: iteration counts, salts, block keys, password verifiers and segment IVs. It may depend on zucrypt and zuxml, never the reverse.
  • zuhttp owns connections, trust and TLS policy and keeps its native OS TLS backends. A bundled TLS engine, if ever taken (Stage 18), is compiled into zucrypt.so, published through a separate table (zucrypt-tls.h) that zuhttp resolves at run time from Suggests:, driven over I/O callbacks zuhttp supplies, verifying only against the CA bundle, host name and pins zuhttp passes. It is never in libzucrypt.a, so ABI 1 never sees it.
  • No encrypt_file(password = ), ever: the package specifies no format.

.agents/design.md (revision 4, 2026-09-29) is the specification and outranks this file; design changes belong there. §3–§8 and §11–§12 describe main; §6, §7.1 and §10 describe where revision 4 takes it (Stages 13–17); §9 and §13 steps 3–5 are plans owned by zuxlsx and zuhttp. .agents/roadmap.md Part A is the plan (its stage map says which stage is current); Part B is the executed v0.1.0 roadmap, kept as the record. Read .agents/stage-1-spike.md before touching src/vendor/, src/Makevars or src/zuc_crypto_config.h.

Current state

Verified 2026-11-09: 0.1.0 is on CRAN, published 2026-10-23 (crandb); it was submitted 2026-09-30 and resubmitted 2026-10-13 from 5a43275, tagged v0.1.0 with its GitHub release. main is 0.1.0.9000. The open version issue is v0.1.1 (#77), with no stage sub-issues yet; the roadmap’s release table plans each tranche as its own minor release (v0.2.0 onwards).

On main, beyond the v0.1.0 surface: Stages 13a (randomness, #9), 14a (AES-GCM and PBKDF2, #10, #12), 15a (RSA and key I/O, #80) and 16a (EC keys, ECDSA, ECDH, X25519, #81) are done. They were split off their tranches because zujwt needed them first. Not built yet: 13b (the rest of tranche 1), 14b (ChaCha20-Poly1305, CTR, padded CBC, HKDF), 15b (envelopes, SSH, fingerprints, bignum, encrypted PEM), 17 (certificates) and 18 (the TLS engine). Stages 15–18 are candidates, each decided when the one before has shipped. Ed25519 is absent from the pinned release: the first documented gap against openssl.

Stability comes in tiers (design §8.6). The seven core R functions of design §7 are stable. The archive (zucrypt.h, libzucrypt.a, ZUCRYPT_ABI_VERSION 1) is frozen as ABI 1 since Stage 11, on zuxlsx’s real decryption core in C (zuxlsx#22 step 3, zuxlsx#64) passing on three operating systems. The table is experimental: no package uses it (#14, #28).

Versions and dependents

The current version’s parent issue is v0.1.1 (#77). Dependents:

  • zuxlsx links the static archive (LinkingTo: zucrypt (>= 0.1.0), no Imports:). revdep.yaml builds it on Linux against every push and pull request, and platforms.yaml on macOS and Windows at the full profile. Every zucrypt release after 0.1.0 is additions only, so none puts zuxlsx back in the release sequence.
  • zujwt is the workflow that admitted Stages 13a–16a.
  • zuhttp is the table consumer that was hoped for, not a real one: its DESCRIPTION has no Imports: and its one pin implementation hashes with the TLS backend’s own SHA-256 (#14).

Deviations from .claude/shared/workflow.md: there is no cran-release.yaml, CRAN-SUBMISSION is git-ignored, and the 0.1.0 tag is v0.1.0, not the bare version. A release is tagged by hand with pkg-post-cran.

A stage that adds or changes a scheduled job closes only after that job’s first real run, dispatched by hand, whose log shows it exercised what it is named for (design §12). Before pushing a stage, document(), test() and check() are clean locally at 0/0/0: CI is for the platforms this machine is not. A failing leg is part of the stage until it is understood, never “unrelated”.

Commands

Beyond the shared devtools commands:

Rscript -e 'devtools::build_readme()'     # README.Rmd -> README.md
Rscript -e 'pkgdown::build_site()'        # site in docs/ (gitignored)
Rscript -e 'pkgbuild::clean_dll()'        # when native state gets stale
Rscript tools/make-kat.R --check          # recompute kat.tsv against openssl
python3 tools/check-kat.py                # aead.tsv, kdf.tsv vs cryptography
python3 tools/make-rsa-kat.py --check     # rsa.tsv, rsa-keys.tsv vs the RFCs
python3 tools/make-ec-kat.py --check      # ec.tsv, ec-keys.tsv vs the RFCs
python3 tools/make-derivation-kat.py ZUXLSX_CHECKOUT --check
sh tools/check-layering.sh                # adapter R-free, glue backend-free
bash tools/check-linking.sh               # the archive, as a consumer links it
make -C ctest run                         # the adapter's C driver (ZUC_CTEST_FULL=1: every alloc)
make -C fuzz replay-run                   # the fuzz corpus through every oracle
make -C fuzz replay-asan                  # the same under ASan + UBSan
tools/ci/platform.sh macos                # platforms.yaml's per-OS checks
tools/vendor/fetch && tools/vendor/record # re-vendor after a keep/patch change
tools/vendor/verify                       # vendored tree vs manifest
R_ENABLE_JIT=0 Rscript tools/alloc-exercise.R [--baseline]
Rscript tools/openssl-usage.R [dir]       # openssl usage by CRAN revdeps

The Python tools need the cryptography package (the derivation one needs msoffcrypto-tool 6.0.0 and a zuxlsx checkout); run them from a venv. Without --check the generators write their fixtures and manifest rows; make-kat.R keeps the rows other generators own. openssl-usage.R is network-bound and backs the tranche order and the migration article’s “N of openssl’s exports”; its results are dated in the roadmap, so re-run it before restating the claim.

Architecture

Three surfaces:

  1. The R surface. The core crypt_* functions (crypt_info(), crypt_hash(), crypt_hmac(), crypt_hex(), crypt_equal(), crypt_rand_bytes(), the crypt_aes_cbc_*_nopad() pair, the crypt_aes_gcm_*() pair, crypt_pbkdf2()) and the openssl-shaped layer (key read and write, RSA, EC, X25519, signatures, crypt_sha*()). The CBC pair carries _nopad (#56) so that Stage 14’s openssl-compatible padded pair can take the ordinary names.
  2. A registered function table (inst/include/zucrypt-r.h, zucrypt_api_v1, resolved lazily via zucrypt_get_api) for consumers with Imports: + LinkingTo: + a real importFrom().
  3. A static archive, libzucrypt.a, for zuxlsx-style consumers (LinkingTo: + configure resolving system.file("lib"), no Imports:). src/install.libs.R installs it to the package’s lib${R_ARCH}/, beside licenses/tf-psa-crypto-LICENSE; there is no inst/lib/ in the sources. It holds the R-free adapter plus vendored crypto, not raw upstream (unlike zukomp/zuxml), so consumers see only inst/include/zucrypt.h.

The native layer is in two halves, and the split is load-bearing. src/zuc_*.c is the adapter: R-free, and what goes into the archive. src/zucrypt_r.c, src/zucrypt_crypt.c, src/zucrypt_api.c and src/zucrypt_test.c are the R glue: backend-free, and not in the archive. src/zucrypt_crypt.c holds the .Call entry points behind the exports. src/zucrypt_test.c is a permanently compiled harness (zucrypt_test_*, the analogue of zukomp’s zu_test_stream()) through which the suite drives the adapter at caller-chosen split points.

An opaque zuc_pkey holds RSA (PKCS#1 DER), EC and X25519 key material, its ptype the backend type, and imports it into PSA per operation, so one key serves every scheme and digest. Randomness reads src/zuc_random.c’s operating-system source directly, not through psa_generate_random().

Naming (design §3, zukomp’s CLAUDE.md is the reference): C ABI prefix zuc_/ZUC_, never zu_ (that is zukomp’s public namespace and zuhttp’s internal one, so a zucrypt.h using it could not be included beside zukomp.h); R exports crypt_*; entry points zucrypt_*; internal zuc_int_*; test-only zucrypt_test_*; condition classes zucrypt_*.

Long-form documentation is pkgdown-only, in vignettes/articles/ (zukomp’s layout), kept out of the tarball. zucrypt.Rmd is “Get started”; c-api.Rmd (“Using zucrypt from C”, #13) quotes the tools/ fixtures, so it moves when they do; backend.Rmd (“The vendored backend”, #17) is what a CRAN or security reviewer reads.

Invariants that are easy to break

  • The ABI 1 promise. Within major version 1, archive functions and table fields may be added, always appended; nothing is removed, reordered or given a new meaning; enumerator values are permanent; and a ZUC_*_REQUIRED_SIZE macro never grows. A layout change to a type struct_size cannot see renames the registered callable instead, so an old consumer fails at R_GetCCallable() rather than reading a moved structure. ?zucrypt_c_api is the published statement.
  • Layering. Including R.h in the adapter compiles fine here and fails much later in a consumer’s build; a backend header in the R glue is the start of PSA types in an installed header. tools/check-layering.sh enforces both directions in CI.
  • inst/include/zucrypt.h compiles standalone as C99 with no R or PSA vocabulary.
  • Upstream symbols are hidden (PKG_CFLAGS = $(C_VISIBILITY)) so independent vendored copies cannot bind to each other; test-abi.R asserts the shared object exports R_init_zucrypt and nothing else.
  • Heap state across a longjmp is owned by R. Every context in src/zucrypt_crypt.c is owned by a finalized external pointer from the moment it exists, created before the context, because the loops call R_CheckUserInterrupt() between 1 MiB chunks. C returns status codes, never Rf_error() below the outermost .Call. src/zuc_live.h counts live handles; test-lifetime.R interrupts each crypt_* loop with setTimeLimit() and checks the count returns to baseline after gc().
  • Key objects are tagged external pointers. Never strip their attributes: an external pointer is not duplicated.
  • Allocation failures are reported as such. The backend allocates through zuc_int_calloc() (MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_CALLOC_MACRO), which records a NULL return; the zuc_pkey_* entry points report any failure after one as ZUC_ERR_MEMORY, because bignum and ASN.1 code turns allocation failures into “invalid key” and the like.
  • The PSA key store is dynamic (MBEDTLS_PSA_KEY_STORE_DYNAMIC, #30): each zuc_aes and zuc_hmac holds one volatile key. The static 32-slot store it replaced failed at the 17th live AES handle as ZUC_ERR_MEMORY. zuc_shutdown() to zero destroys every key, so a test that does it runs with nothing else live.
  • Binary arguments are raw vectors only, except data to crypt_hash() and crypt_hmac(), which may be a connection (#11), streamed in 1 MiB chunks through zucrypt_*_stream_* and refused in text mode. A character value is never a filename, password or byte sequence: a file is hashed as crypt_hash(file(path)). The openssl-shaped layer is the one place character input is accepted, typed as openssl types it.
  • Algorithm names are exact scalars: no partial matching, no fallback.
  • AES wrappers add no padding and no authentication (the CBC pair): keys of 16/24/32 bytes, IVs of exactly 16, data a multiple of 16. The GCM pair is one-shot, with a 12-byte nonce and a 16-byte tag; a received tag of another length is ZUC_ERR_AUTH.
  • Hardware AES stays on. AES-NI or the Arm Cryptography Extension is selected at run time, with table-based software AES as fallback (#51); that fallback leaks key material through cache timing and is documented, not refused; crypt_info()$build_flags$aes_implementation reports the path. Never turn hardware AES off to make platforms “run the same C”: aes-paths.yaml checks each path, including a ZUC_AES_SOFTWARE_ONLY build.
  • SHA-1 is for Office compatibility, never a default for new formats. AES-ECB was removed (#29); it is admissible and in no tranche.
  • openssl compatibility is checked, and subordinate to security. Every mirrored function is byte-identical to openssl, cross-verified, or a documented difference in the migration article; a function in none of the three lists fails the suite. Never mirror a failure to authenticate or verify: openssl 2.3.4’s GCM returns no tag and accepts tampered ciphertext, so crypt_aes_gcm_* keeps RFC 5116’s contract.
  • EC encodings match OpenSSL byte for byte, built in src/zuc_pkey.c: SEC1 with the curve, PKCS#8 around SEC1 without it, RFC 8410 for X25519. ECDSA signatures are raw r || s in C and DER in R, read strictly (the encoding must re-encode identically). zuc_pkey_agree() refuses an all-zero X25519 result.
  • Randomness never uses R’s RNG. test-random.R sets a seed, draws twice and expects a difference.
  • No secrets in conditions. Errors are c(<specific>, "zucrypt_error", "error", "condition"), built in R from a zuc_status mapped by enumerator name. Never attach keys, passwords or plaintext, in the message or the call: zucrypt_abort() reduces every call to the bare function name, because R prints the call with its arguments (#51).
  • API resolution and calls are main-thread only in 0.1.
  • The Office derivation rehearsal is not Office support. It lives in the consumer fixtures and is the ABI validation gate: the generic H_n = hash(int32le(n-1) || H_{n-1}) loop through one reused incremental context, compared with an R loop over crypt_hash() and with one msoffcrypto-tool vector (fixtures/derivation.tsv). No constants, no block keys.
  • Articles run when the site builds, with no Suggests beyond the website needs: mention openssl or sodium in prose, never in a chunk. backend.Rmd’s facts (file counts, defines, sizes, patches) are updated whenever the vendored tree or its configuration changes.
  • Never edit README.md: readme.yaml re-renders it and fails on any difference.

Testing

  • Gate (design §12): published known-answer vectors per algorithm, one-shot vs incremental equivalence, and independent-implementation compatibility. A self round trip is not sufficient. Tests run offline from synthetic fixtures.
  • Fixtures are in tests/testthat/fixtures/ (kat.tsv, aead.tsv, kdf.tsv, rsa*.tsv, ec*.tsv), with provenance in MANIFEST.tsv, read as committed and never regenerated at test time. Generators and oracles are under Commands.
  • Helpers: helper-kat.R (fixture access and zucrypt_test_* harness wrappers), helper-abi.R (symbol audit of the loaded shared object), helper-linking.R (audits of the installed LinkingTo surface, which skip under load_all()). They are helpers rather than file-scope code because testthat’s parallel workers (Config/testthat/parallel: true) source helper-*.R but not a test file’s file scope.
  • zuc_int_random_fail() (src/zuc_live.h) makes the entropy source fail for the harness.
  • The nosuggests leg checks with no Suggests installed, so tests/testthat.R wraps library(testthat) in requireNamespace(). Anything else that reaches for a suggested package from a top-level test or example file is guarded the same way.

Continuous integration

Shared workflows from pedrobtz/r-actions, tracking @v1, except coverage.yaml, pinned to a commit with the tag in a comment. Bump that pin deliberately, reading the diff. Add a workflow at the stage where it has something to check: a job that is green because it inspected nothing is worse than no job.

  • R-CMD-check.yaml: runners plus the clang23, ubuntu-clang and ubuntu-gcc16 containers, nosuggests on.
  • native-checks.yaml: LTO, rchk, gctorture, sanitizers, valgrind, analyzers, cran-special, and the bespoke layering check. rchk and analyzers stay informational until they read zero, then gate with fail-on-findings: true; answer the first false positive with a baseline: file, never by turning the gate off.
  • coverage.yaml (native: true).
  • arch.yaml (weekly): until Stage 8 its legs installed no testthat and ran no tests while green. The Debian legs now install r-cran-testthat and the en_US.UTF-8 locale, Alpine builds testthat (with libuv-dev and linux-headers), and the job sets error-on: warning and require-tests: true.
  • alloc-failure.yaml (weekly): sweeps the allocations of the crypt_* calls only, and compares every result that survives byte for byte with tools/alloc-expected.tsv (written from openssl and hashlib by tools/alloc-expected.R); a namespace loaded inside the window fails the run. expect-pattern lists R’s own out-of-memory wordings, and ignore-crash-pattern R’s regex and gzfile crashes. tools/alloc-exercise.R --baseline runs the prefix so it sits under the floor, and both commands set R_ENABLE_JIT=0, because a failed allocation in R’s own compiler or regex engine crashes R. target-pattern: ZUC_ERR_MEMORY with min-target-hits: 20 proves each run reached the adapter. Needs r-actions >= v1.15.0. The window holds deterministic ECDSA and X25519 only: ECDSA verification and P-256 ECDH allocate 36,000 and 21,000 times and are left out on purpose.
  • vendor.yaml: the vendored tree matches its manifest, and a pull request touching it updates the manifest. vendor-upstream.yaml (weekly) opens an issue when TF-PSA-Crypto releases.
  • Bespoke, adapted from zukomp, because what a package publishes is its own: abi.yaml; consumer.yaml, which builds both fixture packages and fails when zero tests are discovered (any() over an empty vector is FALSE); revdep.yaml, which builds zuxlsx against this checkout and runs its decryption tests; aes-paths.yaml; readme.yaml. These four run on Linux only.
  • platforms.yaml (r-actions’ platforms.yml, weekly) is their macOS and Windows legs, one job per OS, running tools/ci/platform.sh <os>: the headers standalone (macOS), the hardware AES path and the suite against the installed package, both consumer fixtures. At the full profile it adds the fuzz replay (under ASan on macOS) and the zuxlsx revdep. Add a new macOS or Windows check there as a step, never as a new job.
  • fuzz.yaml (own, gated by changes.yml): the corpus in fuzz/corpus/ through every target’s oracle, plain and under ASan + UBSan, on Linux; a 30-second libFuzzer run (600 s at full); and the reach job, whose floor is tools/coverage/floor.dcf. A crash found becomes a regress-<issue>-* seed.
  • mutation.yaml (r-actions’ mutation.yml): Mull over src/zuc_*.c, killed by the C driver in ctest/. Reported and read, never gated; survivors are filed as issues (#126–#130).
  • pkgdown.yaml is this repository’s own, deploying to gh-pages on push to main.
  • assurance.yaml runs r-actions’ assurance.yml, which holds .agents/assurance.md to the portfolio standard: a done check must be backed by a workflow, and a gap must name an issue. Update the file’s rows in the same pull request as a new boundary, object or limit.

The consumer fixtures under tools/ (zukomp’s layout) are unreachable from R CMD check. tools/zucrypttest is the table consumer and calls every table entry, because a pointer never assigned is indistinguishable from a working one until something calls it. tools/zucryptlink is the archive consumer: LinkingTo only, configure/configure.win resolving lib/<arch> then lib/ into a single-quoted PKG_LIBS, exactly as zuxlsx does. tools/check-linking.sh installs it into a library path containing a space, audits that the backend is linked in and that no zuc_/psa_/mbedtls_ symbol is exported from the consumer, checks both copies report the same backend, runs it beside zucrypt.so in both load orders, and with zucrypt removed from the library path. Both fixtures carry the msoffcrypto derivation vector.

Vendored native code

TF-PSA-Crypto 1.1.1 (an LTS branch), Apache-2.0, crypto subset only: no TLS, no X.509 (Stage 17 would need a second vendored library). No Mbed TLS file is vendored: in the 4.x architecture TF-PSA-Crypto is the whole cryptography library. Installation downloads nothing and needs no Python or Perl; the release archive ships the generated sources. The tag, commit, archive checksum, defines and patches are in tools/vendor/manifest.tsv; tools/vendor/verify fails if a vendored file names an author missing from Authors@R or inst/COPYRIGHTS (CRAN’s 2026-10-13 return).

Local patches, in tools/patches/tf-psa-crypto/:

  • 0001-avoid-zero-size-pubkey-array.patch
  • 0002-drop-diagnostic-pragmas.patch
  • 0003-guard-aead-finish-tag-wipe.patch (upstream report: #85)

The configuration is src/zuc_crypto_config.h (forty-eight defines); the trim is 43 objects and 153 files, with aesce.c kept by hand because it has symbols only on Arm. src/Makevars is portable make with an explicit OBJECTS list (no CMake, no GNU make).

Departures from the family layout, both recorded in .agents/stage-1-spike.md: the trim is a two-column keep list (tools/vendor/keep/<source>.txt) rather than a keep_files() case arm, and the tree is flattened to inc/ and lib/ because upstream’s paths exceed the 100-byte tarball limit. The patch record is the manifest’s patches column, not a src/vendor/PROVENANCE. Never edit src/vendor/ in place: change the keep list or add a patch, re-run tools/vendor/fetch and tools/vendor/record, then tools/vendor/verify before committing.
